question: How is fuel carried on the 737-800?

options.text: In two wing tanks and an aft fuselage tank
In two wing tanks and a forward fuselage tank
In a single integral tank across the whole wing
In two main wing tanks and a centre tank

explanation: The wing tanks feed their own engines, and the centre tank is an additional volume used first.

question: How many boost pumps are fitted in each tank?

options.text: One
Two
Three
Four

explanation: A second pump in each tank means the loss of one pump does not affect the supply to the engine.

question: What powers the fuel boost pumps?

options.text: DC electrical power
AC electrical power
The engine driven pump
Engine bleed air pressure

explanation: Because they are AC machines, a total loss of AC generation changes the way the engines are supplied.

question: Why is fuel in the centre tank used before the fuel in the wing tanks?

options.text: The main tank pumps are inhibited until the centre tank has fully run down
A transfer valve moves the centre tank fuel into the wing tanks first
The centre tank pumps deliver a higher output pressure than the main tank pumps
The centre tank pumps are switched on later in the flight by the crew

explanation: The higher pressure simply wins at the manifold, so the sequence happens without any crew action or automatic logic.

question: What is the structural reason for using centre tank fuel first?

options.text: Fuel in the wings relieves the wing bending moment in flight
Centre tank fuel warms more quickly during the cruise
The wing tanks are less well protected against fire
Centre tank fuel is closer to the centre of gravity

explanation: The weight of fuel in the wings acts against the lift, which reduces the bending load at the wing root.

question: Why must the centre tank pumps be switched off when the tank is empty?

options.text: They would prevent the scavenge system from operating
They would interfere with the crossfeed valve operation
They are not cooled by fuel and can be damaged when run dry
They would draw fuel back from the main tanks

explanation: The fuel flowing through the pump is what cools and lubricates it, and running dry is a recognised ignition hazard.

question: What indicates that the centre tank has run down?

options.text: The centre tank pump low pressure lights illuminate
The crossfeed valve opens automatically at that point
The fuel quantity indication for that tank flashes
The main tank pumps increase their output pressure

explanation: The pumps can no longer maintain output pressure, and that loss of pressure is the cue to switch them off.

question: How is each engine normally supplied?

options.text: From the tank on its own side
From whichever tank holds the most fuel
From both tanks through the crossfeed
From the centre tank at all times

explanation: Keeping the feed on its own side is what preserves the lateral balance without crew intervention.

question: What is the purpose of the crossfeed valve?

options.text: It allows either engine to be supplied from either tank
It allows fuel to be jettisoned in an emergency descent
It isolates the centre tank from the fuel manifold
It transfers fuel between the two main wing tanks

explanation: It connects the two sides of the manifold, which is what makes an imbalance correctable and a single tank feed possible.

question: How is a lateral fuel imbalance corrected?

options.text: By opening the crossfeed and switching off all pumps in the heavier tank
By transferring fuel directly from one wing tank to the other
By increasing thrust on the engine with less fuel available
By opening the crossfeed and feeding both engines from the heavier tank

explanation: There is no tank to tank transfer, so the imbalance is removed by burning from the heavier side.

question: Why is there a maximum permitted fuel imbalance between the main tanks?

options.text: Because of the lateral out of balance moment it produces
Because the boost pumps cannot operate below a certain quantity
Because the fuel quantity indication becomes inaccurate
Because the crossfeed valve cannot be opened beyond that difference

explanation: Aileron and trim authority must be able to cope with the asymmetry. Verify the limit against your operator FCOM.

question: What is suction feed?

options.text: The crossfeed manifold drawing fuel from both of the tanks at once together
The engine driven pump drawing fuel from the tank without boost pump assistance
The scavenge system drawing residual fuel out of the centre tank
The APU drawing fuel from the left tank through its own DC pump

explanation: It is the last line of fuel delivery, available because the engine driven pump can lift fuel on its own.

question: What is the principal limitation of suction feed?

options.text: An altitude limit, because fuel vaporises more readily at low pressure
A time limit, because the engine driven pump overheats when unassisted
A requirement for the crossfeed valve to be open throughout
A restriction to the left engine only, since the right has no path

explanation: Vapour in the line interrupts the supply, and the risk increases with altitude and fuel temperature. Verify the limit against your operator FCOM.

question: What is the purpose of the centre tank scavenge system?

options.text: It transfers fuel between the two main tanks
It recovers residual centre tank fuel into a main tank
It returns unburned engine fuel to the centre tank
It removes water from the centre tank sump

explanation: Fuel that the pumps can no longer pick up is still usable, and the scavenge system moves it where it can be used.

question: What is the function of the fuel tank vent system?

options.text: It removes fuel vapour from the tanks continuously to reduce the fire risk in flight
It pressurises the tanks slightly to assist the boost pumps at altitude
It keeps tank pressure close to ambient as fuel is consumed and during climb and descent
It allows water to drain from the tank sumps during the climb and descent

explanation: Without venting, the tank would either collapse inward as fuel is used or burst outward during a climb.

question: What is the purpose of the surge tanks?

options.text: They collect fuel overflow and vent it back to the main tanks
They store a reserve of fuel for the APU to use on the ground
They provide additional capacity for the longer range flights
They separate water from the fuel before it reaches the pumps

explanation: Thermal expansion and manoeuvring can push fuel into the vent lines, and the surge tank catches it rather than losing it overboard.

question: Why are the fuel tank sumps drained before flight?

options.text: Pressure builds up in the tanks overnight and must be relieved before the tanks can be refuelled
The quantity indication must be verified against the contents actually present in each tank
Water settles at the lowest point and must be removed before it can freeze or be drawn into the system
The grade of fuel delivered by the bowser must be checked before it reaches the engines

explanation: Water is denser than fuel and collects at the bottom, which is exactly where the system draws from.

question: Why is a minimum fuel temperature specified?

options.text: Because wax crystals form as the fuel approaches its freezing point and can block the system
Because the fuel quantity indication becomes inaccurate whenever the fuel is very cold
Because the boost pumps are unable to start below that fuel temperature
Because cold fuel increases the risk of a vapour lock forming in the lines

explanation: The limit is tied to the freezing point of the grade uplifted. Verify the limits and the margin against your operator FCOM.

question: How can a low fuel temperature be raised in flight?

options.text: By switching off one boost pump in each main tank
By selecting engine anti-ice on both of the engines
By descending to warmer air or increasing speed
By opening the crossfeed valve for a short period

explanation: Both actions raise the temperature of the air around the tanks and the skin friction heating of the wing surface.

question: From which tank is fuel temperature normally sensed?

options.text: The centre tank
One of the main tanks
The surge tank
The feed manifold

explanation: The main tanks are where the fuel is coldest for longest, since they hold fuel against the wing skin throughout the cruise.

question: What is the risk associated with water in the fuel at altitude?

options.text: It can freeze and restrict the fuel filter or the fuel lines
It accelerates corrosion of the boost pump impellers and casings
It causes the fuel quantity indication to over read
It reduces the calorific value of the fuel burned

explanation: Ice crystals formed from entrained water are a recognised cause of fuel system restrictions in the cruise.

question: What does a fuel filter bypass indication mean?

options.text: The filter has been removed for maintenance and has not been replaced
The filter is restricted and fuel is bypassing it to maintain supply
The boost pump output pressure has fallen below normal
The fuel temperature is below the specified minimum

explanation: Maintaining the flow takes priority over filtration, but the crew must know that unfiltered fuel is reaching the engine.

question: What does a fuel pump LOW PRESSURE light indicate?

options.text: The fuel filter for that side has become restricted
That tank has run down to its last usable fuel
That pump is not delivering its normal output pressure
The crossfeed valve has failed in the closed position

explanation: It refers to the pump, not the tank, which is why the quantity indication has to be read alongside it.

question: Why is the loss of both pumps in one main tank not immediately critical?

options.text: Because the engine driven pump draws from the centre tank instead
Because the engine can be suction fed or supplied through the crossfeed
Because the centre tank pumps take over the supply automatically
Because the scavenge system maintains the supply to that engine

explanation: Two independent alternatives exist, which is why the failure is handled rather than treated as an emergency.

question: How is fuel quantity measured?

options.text: By the flight management computer prediction of the burn
By a float switch in each of the three tanks
By probes in the tanks feeding a quantity indicating system
By flow meters integrating the fuel that is used

explanation: Measuring what is in the tank is independent of what has been burned, which is what allows the two to be compared.

question: Why is the indicated total compared with the flight management computer calculated fuel?

options.text: Because the computer cannot account for the centre tank fuel
Because the computer value is more accurate at low quantities
Because the indication is unavailable below a minimum quantity
Because a growing difference reveals a leak or an indication error

explanation: The tank measurement and the burned fuel calculation are independent, and a divergence between them is the classic leak signature.

question: What is the most important early indication of a fuel leak?

options.text: A fuel pump low pressure light on one of the sides that will not clear when it is reset
An unexplained increase in fuel consumed compared with the plan or an unexpected imbalance
A drop in the fuel temperature in one main tank relative to the other
A fuel filter bypass indication on the engine on the heavier side

explanation: A leak shows itself as fuel disappearing faster than the engines can account for, which is a comparison rather than a warning light.

question: Why should the crossfeed not be used to balance fuel before a suspected leak has been located?

options.text: Because it would disable the fuel quantity indication
Because it may feed the leak from the good tank
Because it increases the fuel consumption of both engines
Because the crossfeed valve cannot be closed once opened

explanation: Connecting the two sides means all the remaining fuel becomes available to whatever is leaking.

question: How is the airplane refuelled?

options.text: Through a pressure connection in the main wheel well
Through a single point refuelling connection under the wing
Through the overwing filler caps on each wing
Through separate connections for each of the tanks

explanation: Pressure refuelling at one point is faster, cleaner and safer than open line refuelling on the wing surface.

question: What is on the refuelling panel?

options.text: The fuel temperature and the boost pump switches
Tank quantity indications and the refuel valve controls
The crossfeed valve control and the pump switches
Tank quantity indications and the jettison controls

explanation: The person refuelling needs to see the quantities and control the valves without entering the flight deck.

question: Can fuel be jettisoned from this airplane?

options.text: Yes, from the centre tank only
Yes, from the main tanks only
Yes, from every tank on board
No, fuel jettison is not fitted

explanation: An overweight landing or a period of holding are the available options, and this shapes the response to an early return.

question: What is the operational consequence of having no jettison capability?

options.text: A diversion airport must always be planned within the first hour of flight
An early return may require an overweight landing or time spent burning fuel
The centre tank cannot be filled at all on the shorter sectors
The airplane is unable to depart at its maximum takeoff weight

explanation: The decision becomes a trade between the urgency of landing and the consequences of landing above the normal weight.

question: What are the fuel measuring sticks used for?

options.text: Sampling the fuel in each of the tanks for water contamination before flight
Checking the calibration of the refuelling panel indications
Measuring the temperature of the fuel in each of the tanks
Determining tank contents manually when the indicating system is unavailable

explanation: A mechanical means of establishing the quantity keeps the airplane dispatchable when the indication fails.

question: Why does fuel density matter when converting volume to mass?

options.text: Because the airplane is loaded by mass while it is delivered by volume
Because the fuel quantity indication measures volume and not mass
Because the boost pumps are calibrated for a specific density
Because the density determines the freezing point of the fuel

explanation: Performance and weight and balance work in mass, and a density assumption error translates directly into a loading error.

question: Why does the usable fuel capacity in mass vary between flights?

options.text: Because the vent system retains a variable quantity in the surge tanks
Because the centre tank capacity depends on the flap setting used
Because the density of the fuel uplifted varies with grade and temperature
Because the tanks expand slightly with the cabin pressurisation

explanation: The tank volume is fixed, so a change in density changes the mass the same volume represents.

question: What is the purpose of the engine fuel shutoff valve controlled by the start lever?

options.text: It admits fuel to the engine and cuts it for shutdown
It selects between the main and the centre tank supply
It isolates the tank from the fuel manifold at the spar
It regulates the fuel pressure delivered to the injectors

explanation: The lever gives the crew a direct means of introducing and cutting fuel independently of the automatic control.

question: Why are there two independent means of cutting fuel to an engine?

options.text: Because the start lever cannot be used once the airplane is airborne
Because one of the valves is electrical and the other is pneumatic
Because the spar valve is used only during the refuelling process
Because a fire requires isolation at the wing as well as at the engine

explanation: Cutting at the engine stops combustion, while cutting at the wing removes the fuel from the line that runs through the pylon.

question: What happens to the fuel supply when an engine fire switch is pulled?

options.text: The spar valve closes, isolating fuel at the wing
The crossfeed valve opens to supply the other engine
The boost pumps in that tank stop automatically
The centre tank pumps are shed from the bus

explanation: Isolating at the spar is what removes the fuel that would otherwise continue to feed a nacelle or pylon fire.

question: Why does the fuel system design keep each engine on its own tank by default?

options.text: To reduce the load carried by the crossfeed manifold
To keep the centre tank available as a reserve supply
To avoid using the crossfeed valve during normal flight
To maintain lateral balance automatically as fuel is burned

explanation: Symmetrical consumption means the crew has nothing to manage unless something abnormal happens.

question: What does the total fuel remaining indication not tell the crew?

options.text: How that fuel is distributed and whether all of it is usable
The quantity that is held in each of the individual tanks
The mass of the fuel that is actually on board
The fuel that has been used since the departure

explanation: Fuel trapped in a tank whose pumps have failed is counted in the total but may not reach an engine.

question: Why is the fuel state assessed as usable fuel rather than total fuel after a system failure?

options.text: Because the reserve fuel is excluded from the indicated total figure
Because a pump or valve failure can make part of the load unavailable
Because the quantity indication is degraded after a failure
Because the centre tank is never counted as usable fuel

explanation: The decision about where the airplane can go depends on what can actually reach the engines.

question: What is the effect of losing all AC electrical power on the fuel system?

options.text: The crossfeed valve opens automatically to join the tanks
The fuel is supplied by the APU DC powered pump instead
The boost pumps stop and the engines rely on suction feed
The engines shut down when the manifold pressure falls

explanation: The engine driven pump continues to work mechanically, which is why the loss of the boost pumps is not the loss of the engines.

question: Why does a total AC failure introduce an altitude consideration?

options.text: Because suction feed becomes less reliable as altitude increases
Because the vent system cannot maintain the tank pressure up there
Because the fuel temperature falls more quickly at altitude
Because the centre tank cannot then be isolated from the rest

explanation: Fuel vaporises more readily at low ambient pressure, and the engine driven pump cannot handle vapour.

question: What is the purpose of the fuel used indication?

options.text: It shows the difference in quantity between the two main tanks
It shows the fuel remaining in each of the individual tanks
It shows the fuel still required to reach the destination
It shows how much fuel each engine has consumed since it was reset

explanation: Comparing consumption between engines can reveal a leak or an engine problem before any warning appears.

question: What would an increasing difference in fuel used between the two engines suggest?

options.text: That the crossfeed valve has opened without being selected
A normal consequence of flying with asymmetric thrust set
A leak or an abnormality on one side that requires investigation
A fault in the fuel quantity indicating system on one side

explanation: The two engines at the same thrust setting should burn at closely similar rates, and a growing difference has a cause.

question: What is the function of the fuel manifold?

options.text: It vents fuel vapour from the tanks to the surge tanks
It connects the tank supplies so any tank can feed any engine
It measures the fuel flow delivered to each engine
It separates water from the fuel before it is delivered

explanation: It is the common gallery the pumps deliver into, and the crossfeed valve is what divides or joins it.

question: Why is the fuel configuration checked before descent and approach?

options.text: Because the boost pumps must all be switched off before landing
Because the centre tank must contain a minimum quantity then
Because the remaining fuel must be usable and balanced for the landing
Because the crossfeed valve must be open for a go around

explanation: A go around at low fuel state with an imbalance or an unavailable tank is not the moment to discover a configuration problem.

question: Which fuel grades are approved for this airplane type?

options.text: Aviation gasoline grades such as AVGAS 100LL
Automotive gasoline of 95 octane or higher
Kerosene grades such as Jet A and Jet A-1
Diesel and kerosene mixtures in any proportion

explanation: The engines are gas turbines, which are designed around the properties of kerosene.

question: What is the purpose of a fuel system icing inhibitor additive where it is used?

options.text: It prevents microbial growth from developing in the fuel tanks
It raises the flash point of the fuel that is uplifted
It increases the calorific value of the fuel uplifted
It lowers the temperature at which entrained water forms ice crystals

explanation: It addresses the water in the fuel rather than the fuel itself, which is where the icing problem actually originates.

question: Why is the centre tank quantity relevant to the takeoff configuration?

options.text: Because the centre tank has to be completely empty before the takeoff
Because centre tank fuel is not counted in the takeoff weight
Because the pumps must be correctly selected for the quantity actually loaded
Because the centre tank quantity affects the flap setting that is required

explanation: Running the pumps in an empty tank, or leaving them off with fuel loaded, are both configuration errors made before departure.

question: What does the fuel quantity indicating system display when a probe fails?

options.text: A value computed from the fuel flow to that engine
The last valid value recorded for that tank
Nothing, since the system reverts to a total only
A degraded or flagged indication for the affected tank

explanation: A flagged indication prompts the crew to establish the quantity by another means rather than trusting a wrong number.

question: Why is the fuel load cross checked against the flight plan requirement before departure?

options.text: Because the centre tank must always be the last to be filled in the refuelling sequence
Because the fuel quantity indication drifts while the airplane is on the ground
Because the two main tanks have to be filled symmetrically before departure
Because an error in uplift or in density can leave the airplane short of the required fuel

explanation: The check compares two independently produced figures, which is what catches a uplift or conversion error before it matters.

question: What is the significance of the low fuel warning in a main tank?

options.text: It indicates that both of the boost pumps in that tank have failed and stopped delivering
It indicates that the centre tank has run down and its pumps must be switched off
It indicates an imbalance between the two main tanks that must now be corrected
It indicates the quantity has fallen to a level requiring immediate attention to the fuel state

explanation: It is a quantity warning rather than a system warning, and it exists because fuel state errors develop slowly and quietly.

question: Why does the fuel system have no tank to tank transfer capability?

options.text: Because the vent system could not cope with the flow rates that a transfer needs
Because transfer pumps and their plumbing would add unacceptable weight
Because the tanks are at different structural levels within the wing
Because the crossfeed and the consumption sequence are sufficient to manage balance

explanation: Managing the burn is simpler and lighter than moving fuel around, which is why the design solves imbalance by consumption.

question: What must be confirmed before opening the crossfeed valve to correct an imbalance?

options.text: That both of the engines are set to the same thrust setting at the time
That the airplane has descended below the transition level
That the centre tank pumps have both been switched off
That the cause of the imbalance is understood and a leak has been excluded

explanation: The action is safe when the imbalance is due to consumption and dangerous when it is due to a leak.
